newsitem.title: CHINA: Hungry North Korea braces for difficult summer.
newsitem.headline: Hungry North Korea braces for difficult summer.

text.p: North Korea, hit by floods, failed harvests and chronic food shortages, is bracing for its most difficult summer in years of economic decline, a United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) official said on Wednesday.

Grain imports and foreign food aid to the reclusive communist nation would become even more vital as hungry North Koreans exhausted food stocks, said Arthur Holcombe, Beijing resident representative for the UNDP.

"After June of 1997 and up until the next harvest in September there will be essentially no grain crop available for the population," Holcombe told a seminar on North Korea organised by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of Beijing.

"It looks at the moment to be a period of particular hardship," he said, adding the summer was likely to be North Korea's hardest in seven years of decline since the collapse of former ally the Soviet Union.

North Korea's food shortages and the slow implosion of its Stalinist economy are not the only problems facing Pyongyang, which was hit last month by the defection of the architect of its ruling ideology of strict self-reliance.
Defector Hwang Jang-yop has been holed up in the South Korean mission to Beijing since he plunged ties between China and the two hostile Koreas into crisis by seeking asylum there on February 12.

Hwang's defection and recent political reshuffles indicated the Pyongyang leadership was in crisis, said Krzysztof Darewicz of the Polish Press Agency, one of a tiny band of correspondents accredited to North Korea.
"There is growing uncertainty in the leadership," Darewicz told the seminar, adding that North Korean political collapse appeared increasingly likely.
The UNDP's Holcombe said grain shipments to North Korea from China and other countries and proposed barter deals would be vital to fill a huge gap in the hermit nation's food supplies.
North Korea's grain output had declined an annual four percent since 1990 and farmers had been further hit in recent years by a string of natural disasters, he said.
Floods in 1995 and 1996 drowned rice fields, washed away roads and left half a million North Koreans homeless out of a population of 23 million, relief organisations say.
"Last September there was a 1.8 million tonne grain deficit... and they haven't found half of that," Holcombe said.
Aid agencies have warned of potential famine in North Korea, although they say that international aid, rationing and the nation's efficient food distribution system have so far averted starvation.
While food supplies over the summer months remained precarious, there were signs that Pyongyang was becoming more open to the outside world, Holcombe said.

The Rajin-Sonbong Free Economic and Trade Zone near the Tumen River border with China and Russia was having growing success in attracting foreign investors, said Ian Davies of the UNDP's Tumen River Area Development Programme.
Total investment in the zone was expected to soar to around $150 million by the end of 1997 from just $20 million at the end of 1995, he said.
